Good Thursday morning. This is Sam Francis.

RIOT, ACT: The government will respond this morning to a second consecutive night of disorder in the second week in which riots have broken out on U.K. streets. A flurry of announcements came in last night on increasing immigration enforcement, police reinforcements flown in from Britain and regulatory threats against Elon Musk’s X.

The obvious side effect … is that one week before the Makerfield by-election, the aftermath of Monday’s knife attack in Belfast is dominating the little remaining news bandwidth available to Keir Starmer, just as some of the other big ticket policies his government was working on appear to drag. More on that issue below. But first …

Benn there: Northern Ireland Secretary Hilary Benn is dialing into the morning broadcast round from Belfast and facing questions on how quickly the government can restore order — and whether it can move faster than disorder spreads online. Timings as ever below. We could expect Benn to visit affected areas and attend potential meetings with police, though his movements weren’t nailed down last night.

**A message from Palantir: At Palantir, what we value is helping our customers deliver better public services. Our software is driving up NHS operations, speeding up cancer diagnosis, tackling crime, preventing domestic violence and helping our armed forces protect our security. 17 per cent of our workforce is based here in the UK - and that’s what makes them tick.**

Robinson Crusade: The second night of violence was triggered after the suspect in Monday’s horrifying knife attack was named as Hadi Alodid, a 30-year-old refugee from Sudan. The same online agitators who whipped up Southampton’s riots after the Henry Nowak verdict — with Tommy Robinson once again to the fore — have been folding what appear to be two very different attacks into a single anti-migrant narrative.

Last night in Belfast: There were fewer incidents than 24 hours ago and no repeat of occupied buildings being set alight. But disorder continued, vehicles were seen in flames and a crowd attempted to set fire to a derelict property in the same area. Police used water cannon to repel the crowds and again came under attack from bricks, stones and bottles. The violence came despite a plea from the family of Stephen Ogilvie — who lost an eye in the attack — urging “peaceful protests” and saying the unrest was “not welcome.” The Telegraph reports Ogilvie remains in a coma after being stabbed in the face, neck and back.

Doth protest too much: More than 100 people appeared to have been tricked into coming to the Stormont estate in Belfast for an anti-immigration protest that didn’t take place. One attendee told the BBC they believed “somebody had just made a poster up” and shared it on social media. “It’s a total waste of time,” they added. The crowd dispersed without incident.

FRONT PAGE NEWS: The papers this morning are once again dominated by the violent disorder in Belfast — as well as tricky details for the government (and the Tories, who were in charge at the time) about the immigration rules that allowed Alodid to arrive in the U.K. The Times’ David Shipley and Matt Dathan report an asylum caseworker describing how it was “supremely easy” for Sudanese nationals to secure protection at the time Alodid arrived in early 2023, amid pressure to clear claims quickly.

Weakest link: A second Times scoop by Dathan reveals Home Office insiders describing the Common Travel Area as “a massive Achilles’ heel” in border security, allowing illegal migrants to take advantage of the lack of routine immigration checks. It’s part of a story about how the previous government managed to send just one asylum-seeker back to Ireland under the now-defunct post‑Brexit returns deal.

Achilles’ heel indeed: The Telegraph’s Charles Hymas and Mitchell Durdin report smugglers openly advertising the route believed to have been used by Alodid, billing it as a “guaranteed” way into Britain. Albanian gangs have been promoting the journey on TikTok — flying into Dublin, crossing into Northern Ireland, then traveling on to England — as a safer alternative to Channel crossings, exploiting the lack of routine checks.

Hall that: The independent reviewer of terrorism legislation, Jonathan Hall, appears in both the Times and the Telegraph warning immigration needs to be treated as a national security issue. In an op-ed in the Times, Hall warns that while British nationals still dominate terror-arrest statistics, the government’s human rights approach to migration was failing to deal with the tensions leading to violent disorder across the U.K.

Government line: Officials insisted to Playbook overnight that immigration enforcement in Northern Ireland was being intensified before this week’s disorder, pointing to 1,000 removals of illegal migrants over the past year. They are also keen to stress the longer term: £3.7 billion earmarked for Immigration Enforcement over the next three years, with spending set to rise by more than 20 percent by 2028/29.

Safety dance: Last night Ofcom confirmed it had contacted X and other platforms after Technology Secretary Liz Kendall explicitly asked the watchdog to discuss with the companies how they plan to comply with the Online Safety Act, warning some of the violence “appears to have been incited online.” Kendall had promised to give Ofcom greater powers to impose penalties on platforms that fail to proactively remove harmful content next week (we covered much of this in Playbook PM). The coming days could offer a useful test of how far the watchdog is willing — and legally able — to push social media companies, before the government unveils a tranche of tougher social media restrictions in its response to the consultation on keeping children safe online.

X marks the spot: The former CEO of the National Cyber Security Centre, Ciaran Martin, told Times Radio the government should either “stop using X or stop moaning about it” — not on security grounds, but because it is “mad” for the state to be producing vast amounts of content and effectively handing it to the platform while Musk monetizes the traffic.

Elon Musk’s response … so far has been to continue amplifying people defending the disorder and calling Keir Starmer a racist.

GOOD TIMING: The government is due to publish fresh figures at 9.30 a.m. on the number of successful and unsuccessful asylum appeals. One to watch for how the system is performing.

ZIA LATER: All of this gives Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf plenty of material for tonight, when he appears online with the Trump‑adjacent Heritage Foundation. He is set to be interviewed at 10 p.m. U.K. time by its London‑based director, Nile Gardiner. The question is whether Yusuf sticks to Nigel Farage’s line, condemning the violence in Belfast while arguing most involved are “not far-right, not extremists, just really scared” about events in their communities and a lack of government response.

YOU’VE LOST THE NEWS: Today had been penciled in across Westminster for the long‑awaited Defence Investment Plan. It is now pushed back to next week at the earliest, Playbook and others hear. And POLITICO reports this morning that Starmer’s planned EU reset is also in trouble. Together, the deals were supposed to be two major pillars of Starmer’s don’t-call-it-a-legacy push. Nothing is easy, even in Starmer’s get-sh*t-done era.

SCOOP — Youth in revolt: My colleague Anne McElvoy reports that the planned U.K.-EU summit has been thrown into jeopardy after talks got stuck on youth visas. The talks are a central part of the U.K.’s attempted trade reset with continental Europe, 10 years after the Brexit vote. But officials from both sides tell POLITICO that some EU members —Brussels will not say which — are threatening to block or water down the plan, amid fears over its effect on their own labor markets. That means some doubt over the target date of July 13. Check out Anne’s full story here, and there’ll be more on the Politics at Sam and Anne’s podcast out shortly.

Don’t hold your breath: Meanwhile, Defence Secretary John Healey all but confirmed the Defence Investment Plan ain’t happening this week. He told a press conference last night that the government would “respect parliament” after Speaker Lindsay Hoyle kicked off about it potentially landing on a non-sitting Friday. Healey and Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper also declined to rule out tax rises to fund the military, as they were peppered with DIP questions at a joint appearance with Australian counterparts.

Bless this mess: POLITICO’s Mason Boycott‑Owen texted in late last night to say some sort of defense announcement is still expected on Friday — just not the fully costed DIP. The fact Playbook was still getting updates on what might land late into the night tells you how messy things have become.

Bye the DIP? Sky’s Deborah Haynes revealed last night that Chief of the Defence Staff Richard Knighton has written directly to Starmer amid reports the Treasury offered just around £13 billion to fund the DIP — roughly £5 billion short of what national security adviser Jonathan Powell wanted, and barely half the £28 billion gap identified in the Strategic Defence Review. The content of the missive isn’t known, but it doesn’t appear to be a love letter. Officials didn’t deny the account when approached by Playbook, instead pointing to the government’s line that the government had overseen “the biggest sustained increase in defense spending since the Cold War.”

That could complicate things: The Telegraph reports Ed Miliband has been resisting No. 10 demands for at least 1 percent capital cuts to help fund the long-delayed DIP. Could this be a power battle between Starmer and his more Burnham-curious ministers?

KEIR FORCE ONE: All of this is unfolding as the Makerfield by‑election — effectively the starting gun on any leadership contest — hurtles into view. The Guardian’s lobby team have a good read on how Starmer’s aides are war-gaming out how to survive Andy Burnham’s expected return to Westminster, including the possibility of sacking ministers who back him for leader (as the FT reported earlier in the week). One Burnham ally told the paper Starmer was “like a dog barking in an empty room,” where eventually the “owner is going to come back home and kick it out.” Oof.

Sting in the tale: The policy questions are hardly easy for Burnham either, of course. The Greater Manchester mayor may already have signed up to his first multi‑billion pound pledge if he becomes PM — saying more than 3.5 million WASPI women “deserve” compensation. The comments at a Wednesday hustings, splashed on the front page of the FT, revive a row Starmer’s team has spent months trying to close down on cost grounds, with potential payouts estimated at up to £10.5 billion. A Starmer supporter told Playbook last night the story reminds people exactly why Burnham “lost two leadership elections and why Keir won a landslide general election.” Ouch.

Burnham notice: Analysis from my colleague John Johnston suggests Burnham has shifted his campaign strategy sharply in the closing stretch, zeroing in on hyper‑local issues. Around £8,000 has gone into Meta ads over the past week, pushing pledges on cleaning up a local dump, new link roads and opening a pharmacy and GP surgery. It is a notable pivot from the “change Labour” message aimed at Westminster and party members — and a sign Reform’s attacks, accusing Burnham of using Makerfield as a “stepping stone” in his quest for high office, are landing.

Bounced by Belfast: The Telegraph’s Nick Gutteridge reckons the horrific attack in Belfast may end up costing Burnham the Makerfield race by pushing an immigration debate to the top of the agenda in the final stretch. His reporting draws on focus group work suggesting local voters already think Labour looks weak on the issue. (Though a caveat: the focus group was held weeks ago, well before Monday night’s attack and the unrest that followed.)

Lowe and behold: The i Paper’s Kitty Donaldson reports polling doing the rounds amongst Labour staffers suggests Burnham is on course to win — helped by a split on the right. Rupert Lowe’s hard‑right Restore party is put on 13 percent, cutting into Reform’s vote, which sits at around 24. (Reform officials insist the Restore total is way lower). Lowe is also trying to build out his ranks, with Donaldson reporting he is seeking to recruit former Reform MP James McMurdock, now an independent following allegations of financial misconduct.

ANOTHER SILVER LINING FOR LABOUR: Party aides are confident that the government will change the law in time to hold any Greater Manchester by-election under the “supplementary vote” system — not first past the post, POLITICO’s Dan Bloom texts in to say.

That’s numberwang: SV is likely to benefit Labour because the system leads to more votes broadly on the left coalescing around one party. It used to be used for mayoral elections until the Tories scrapped it in 2022. The legislation to reverse that move is working its way through the system now and was considered by a committee of MPs in recent days.

LOVE LOST: Labour deputy leader and senior Burnham ally Lucy Powell used the ThinkLabour (formerly Labour Together) summer reception to vent some frustration at the state of her party, lamenting that instead of debating “big ideas,” attention had turned to “the moves of three men — or maybe it’s two men now.” She asked that any leadership rivals make their moves in “a few less football kits and tight shorts.” Powell also praised Alison Phillips, the new think tank CEO, saying “for women in politics, a lot of what we do is clear up the mess that the men leave behind … Alison’s doing a great job of that as well.” Ahem.

JUST DO IT: Met Police Commissioner Mark Rowley is piling pressure on Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to introduce legislation that’d force tech firms to turn any phone stolen in the U.K. into a useless brick, my tech reporter colleague Mizy Clifton texts in. Rowley is due on a broadcast media round this morning (timings below).

Brick by brick: Apple has already agreed to tighten protections to make stolen iPhones harder to reactivate and to share device identifiers with the Met — a move Rowley says is already “making a difference.”  The Daily Mail is also claiming credit. The firm has made some of these changes globally though, which perhaps suggests it’s not all down to the U.K.

THE DOCTOR WILL SEE YOU NOW: It’s also a big day for Health Secretary James Murray, who will start his morning bracing for NHS stats to drop (all at 9.30 a.m.) including A&E attendances and emergency admissions, waiting times for suspected and diagnosed cancer patients and diagnostic waiting times.

But wait, there’s more: He also has a visit to a northwest hospital before his first pool interview in the new job. He’ll then make a speech at the NHS Confederation Expo (livestream here) at 3 p.m., followed by a fireside chat. And he has penned a piece for LabourList about his first month in the health brief — which some could read as a pitch to keep him in DHSC for the long run. Best of luck.

Scan do attitude: Murray has also found some more of the AI the government likes and will talk up an announcement of £20 million being put into rolling out AI-powered chest X-ray tools to every NHS trust in England by 2029. Using AI as a “second pair of eyes” in half NHS England has helped helping more than 4 million receive a faster diagnosis already, the government says.

SCOOP — VOTE OF NO CONFIDENCE: The wave of anti-incumbent anger that kicked out governments across the world in 2024 has, surprisingly, not gone away according to a poll carried out for POLITICO. Voters in Britain and America are not just grumpy with the last lot, with 71 percent of U.S. respondents claiming politicians only look out for themselves. Meanwhile 45 percent of Brits say the country keeps changing prime ministers because “none of them are any good.”

MAKE YOURSELF COMFORTABLE: Chancellor Rachel Reeves plans to address so-called double or triple taxation faced by wealthy U.S. expats who are both British residents and members of U.S. limited liability companies, Bloomberg’s Joe Mayes reports.

EASY BEING GREEN: The government has put £240 million behind the revamped Sustainable Farming Incentive, insisting it’s now simpler, fairer and comes with less red tape.

PING: Smartphones have destroyed Westminster and my colleague Charlie Cooper has a fascinating piece on the topic in which many MPs sound like they would like to throw their devices into the Thames. Former No. 10 comms boss James Lyons bemoaned the “instant gratification culture” that phones have built, which “doesn’t lend itself to … long-term fixes for the country.”

DON’T LOOK BACK IN ANGER: Reform UK has dug up a letter that Kemi Badenoch wrote as equalities minister, in which she describes the Public Sector Equality Duty — which she has now said she’d scrap — as an “important” part of government, ensuring that “fairness is at the heart of everything we do.” A Reform official accused her of “enforcing the policy she now says is damaging.” Farage has posted an excerpt of the letter to hammer home the point … you can read the full letter here.

REPORTS OUT TODAY: Eighty-three percent of Brits think wealthy individuals use political donations to influence the government for their own personal interests, according to polling from Transparency International … DESNZ has accepted the Environmental Audit Committee’s call to give MPs a half-day of debate in the Commons to agree the next carbon budget.

A BUGS LIFE: UKHSA has published its first proper league table of things that could make Britain very ill — and pandemic-capable respiratory infections like Covid-19 are still top. The new Health Security Risk Assessment gives ministers and health chiefs “reasonable worst-case scenarios” for the next five years, from a novel flu infecting more than half the population to declining childhood jabs, extreme heat and antimicrobial resistance making old threats nastier. You cannot say you were not warned this time.

HOUSE OF COMMONS: Sits from 9.30 a.m. with transport questions … business questions to Leader of the House Alan Campbell … and a general debate on the legacy of Jo Cox. Labour MP Joe Powell has the adjournment debate on the ninth anniversary of the Grenfell Tower fire.

HOUSE OF LORDS: Sits from 11 a.m., with questions on drafting a bill creating the legal framework for the proscription of the IRGC, tackling antisemitism in the U.K. and the Social Market Foundation report, “No news is bad news: The hidden threat of unchecked local misinformation” … a debate on welfare reforms and youth unemployment … a short debate on the Political and security situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina … and a debate on the rural economy.

THE ULTIMATE SPOTTED: The i Paper’s Richard Holmes has got his hands on photos of Russian tech boss Aleksei Kolotilov, the creator of a hyper-realistic simulator for piloting kamikaze drones, on holiday at Disneyland Paris. Kolotilov has been able to go on a string of family holidays across the U.S. and Europe during the Ukraine war, raising questions about the ability of Western authorities to tackle Russian actors.

IS THIS THE PLAN? U.S. forces launched a second straight day of airstrikes in Iran Wednesday as Donald Trump presses for a settlement to end the war, my POLITICO colleagues report. Tehran fired at American bases in the region and the two sides traded claims about whether ships could pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

BUSY: Trump will not attend the first U.S.-based match of the FIFA World Cup between the U.S. and Paraguay on Friday in LA, my POLITICO colleagues report.

NOT FOR ME: Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates told the U.S. House Oversight and Government Reform Committee that he was “never interested” in having a personal friendship with Jeffrey Epstein and said he cut off ties with him in 2014 when it became clear the donors the financier promised to deliver would not be making contributions to Gates’ philanthropic work.

Details: Gates also said that Epstein learned “sensitive information about my personal life, including the fact that I had been unfaithful in my marriage,” and used it “to pressure me to re-engage with him. He was unsuccessful in this effort, but it shows some of the ways he tried to leverage his interactions with me to further his agenda.”

**A message from Palantir: Palantir software is helping to deliver better patient care - including 110,000 additional operations to date, a 15% reduction in discharge delays, a 6.8% increase in the number of patients finding out whether they need cancer treatment within 28 days, and the safe removal of 797,728 patients from waiting lists. The same software is helping police forces in England to tackle crime too. The Metropolitan Police have used it to identify misconduct within the force and arrest officers. It has helped Bedfordshire Police to reduce the time taken to check whether someone’s partner has a history of violence by 85 per cent, identifying 1,000 vulnerable women in a single year. It is also being used to bring organised crime gangs such as F*** the Police to justice. A stronger NHS and safer streets. Values we can all agree on.**
